sections.h2: Ways to sell a McDonough house
sections.html:
A McDonough owner can hand the sale to an agent, run it personally, or sell to a cash buyer who takes the house in its present condition. Each route trades price, time and effort differently.

With an agent you reach the widest pool of buyers, though the closing date follows the buyer's financing. Selling it yourself means no agent on your side, so pricing, paperwork and walk-throughs are yours. A cash purchase has fewer contingencies and no repair demands, which helps with inherited houses, tenant problems or payments that have fallen behind.

Whatever you choose, get terms in writing, including who pays the state transfer tax and how property tax is settled at closing.

McDonough is the seat of Henry County, about thirty miles southeast of Atlanta, and it has grown quickly. It counted 22,084 residents in 2010 and 29,051 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 33,395, which is 14.5% above the April 2020 estimates base of 29,178.

Owners occupy 54.8% of homes, and a typical owned home is valued at $314,600. Owning with a mortgage costs about $1,791 a month, and gross rent is $1,792. Median household income is $75,343 across 10,886 households of about 2.76 people each. A family-sized house with room for that many people fits the local demand, but your own house will price by its condition and location.

McDonough's Building and Inspection Division reviews plans and issues permits so that construction meets municipal code. Work that builds, enlarges, alters, repairs, moves or demolishes a structure needs a permit, and so does installing or replacing electrical, gas, mechanical, plumbing or sprinkler systems. Georgia law, O.C.G.A. 43-14, sets trade requirements for plumbing, electrical and heating-air work, and the city says the same applies to homeowners doing that work themselves.

McDonough permit and code contacts
ServiceContact or timing
Next-day inspectionCall 678-782-6217 before 4 p.m.; later calls are scheduled two days out

Friday or holiday calls before 4 p.m. for an inspection go to the next working day.

The city enforces the current Georgia State Minimum Codes for Construction published by the Department of Community Affairs, including the International Residential Code, the International Energy Conservation Code, the National Electrical Code and the International Property Maintenance Code. Water and sewer tap applications and an irrigation meter application are on the Building Division's forms page, as is an Owner Occupied Housing Rehabilitation Program application. The same page separates residential from commercial permit applications and posts a fee schedule, so pull the residential form and fee list if you are unsure what an earlier repair required.

Code Compliance sits inside the Planning and Zoning Division of Community Development. Officers usually notify the person responsible, explain how to fix the violation and allow a set time. If voluntary efforts fail, a citation sends the matter to McDonough Municipal Court. The Mayor and Council adopt the codes but do not handle individual cases.

A house with an open violation can still be sold, but the cleanest path is to resolve it first. Ask about a case through the hotline at 470-878-1150.

Before listing, check that decks, water heaters, additions or finished basements were permitted. Work done without the proper permits can be penalized, and a buyer's inspector may ask for proof.

Henry County's Tax Assessor handles the Notice of Assessment, property appeals, homestead exemption, conservation use and property returns. Georgia's appeal statute, O.C.G.A. 48-5-311, sets the written appeal window at 45 days after the notice date. A McDonough owner follows the same statewide process, so go by the date printed on your own notice.

The notice shows the assessed value and an estimate of taxes, so keep it with your sale papers. Before choosing a closing date, request your current bill, due dates and balance from the Henry County Tax Commissioner, and ask the Tax Assessor which exemptions your house carries.

A homestead exemption belongs to the seller and ends at the sale, so the buyer files a new application for their own after closing.

sections.h2: What the county needs to see before closing
sections.html: Get the current bill and any balance from the Tax Commissioner, and the exemption list from the Tax Assessor. Confirm that your house sits inside McDonough city limits, since the city's permit and code rules apply only there. Your closing attorney will ask for the same items, so having them ready keeps a sale on its schedule, whether the buyer pays cash or uses a loan.

sections.h2: How a McDonough sale moves from offer to closing
sections.html:
1. Gather the deed, a mortgage payoff figure and your latest tax notice.
  2. Check that permits for any deck, addition or finished basement were closed out.
  3. Settle or answer any code case before the buyer's inspector finds it.
  4. Agree in writing who pays the transfer tax and how the tax bill is split.
  5. Close with an attorney, who has the deed recorded after the state tax is paid.

A cash sale cuts out the lender's appraisal and the repair requests that often come with one, so steps two and three matter less to that buyer, though a price adjustment may stand in for them. A listing sale gives you more buyers, and the buyer's lender sets the pace.

Tenants and inheritance questions should be raised early with any buyer, because buyers price in uncertainty. A house with a tenant in place or an unsettled estate takes longer on any route.

sections.h2: Transfer tax on a McDonough sale
sections.html:
The Henry County Clerk of Superior Court records deeds after the state tax is paid. That tax is $1 for the first $1,000 of price or any fraction thereof, plus 10 cents per additional $100 or fraction thereof.

The seller is liable under O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10, though many sales contracts make the buyer pay. The PT-61 form is filled out online with the state clerks' cooperative, and a printed copy goes to the clerk with the deed. Exemption questions belong with the Henry County clerk.

faqs.q: Is an open McDonough code violation a barrier to selling?
faqs.a: Yes, though the cleanest path is to resolve it first. Code Compliance normally gives the responsible person time to fix a violation and cites them to Municipal Court if that fails. Ask about a case at 470-878-1150.

faqs.q: How soon can I get a building inspection in McDonough?
faqs.a: Call the inspection request line at 678-782-6217 before 4 p.m. for a next-day inspection. Requests after 4 p.m. are scheduled two days out.

faqs.q: What is a typical home worth in McDonough?
faqs.a: A typical owned home is valued at $314,600, with 54.8% of homes owner-occupied. Your own house will price by its condition and location.

faqs.q: Who owes transfer tax in a McDonough sale?
faqs.a: The statute puts it on the seller, and many contracts shift it. Read yours, and ask the Henry County clerk if an exemption might apply. The state form is filed electronically.

faqs.q: What should I ask Henry County before closing on my McDonough house?
faqs.a: Get the current bill and any balance from the Tax Commissioner, and the exemption list from the Tax Assessor. Also confirm your house sits inside city limits.
